reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents a BNB flash-loan arbitrage/front-run tutorial as a way to earn easy profits and free BNB without collateral. It instructs viewers to connect a MetaMask wallet, set a large loan amount, and send BNB to a contract as fees, while claiming that larger payments produce larger returns and reporting more than 3.8 BNB received. Binance-branded imagery and general warnings about flash-loan exploits provide context, but the available video evidence does not establish Binance affiliation, actual execution results, recipient ownership, victim losses, or what the contract does after confirmation.

citations.quote: BNB Flash Loan Arbitrage Tutorial Front Run Bot 2022 Update | Easy Profits in Minutes!
Flash loan arbitrage tutorial to get FREE BNB with no collateral using a BNB flash loan attack
Connect your wallet when prompted (Metamask Preferable)
Enter your token details and deploy the contract (MyToken)
Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps

opening.argument: Judge, the description does not present flash loans as risk-free. It explicitly warns that exploits have caused serious losses and says the contract may fail when the amount sent is too low. It also explains the requested BNB as fees for swaps and notes that fees vary. Those statements do not prove the procedure works, but they are relevant to how the video presents it: as a technical process with costs and failure conditions, not an unconditional promise of payment.

citations.quote: flash loan exploits have been used to attack vulnerable DeFi protocols and steal millions of dollars.
Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
fees may be different from day to day.
Avoid using very low amounts as contract may fail below 0.15 BNB

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening rightly identifies a wallet connection and a BNB transfer, but those steps alone do not establish where the funds ultimately go or whether the contract diverts them. The description identifies the transfer as a fee for swaps and acknowledges that execution can fail. The profit language deserves skepticism; it does not erase the stated costs and limitations.

citations.quote: Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
Avoid using very low amounts as contract may fail below 0.15 BNB

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warning concerns exploits against DeFi protocols, not the viewer's risk of sending BNB to this contract. Failure below a fee threshold is not a meaningful qualification of the return claim. The description instructs viewers to send BNB and then call the contract's action function, while the narration claims larger payments yield larger returns. Uncertainty about the eventual recipient does not make that solicitation an ordinary risk disclosure.

citations.quote: Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
Call “action” function.
The more BNB you send the more you get

opening.argument: Judge, the central format is a software walkthrough. The speaker tells viewers to create a Solidity file, paste code, configure the compiler and connect a wallet; the description continues through deployment and calling a function. That is substantive operational instruction, not just a demand to send money. The speaker's claimed result should be treated as an unverified demonstration claim, but its presence does not by itself establish that the walkthrough is a deceptive solicitation.

citations.quote: Go to remix.ethereum.com, create a file, and name it contract.sol
Step 4: Click compile contract.sol
Step 7: Connect your wallet when prompted (Metamask Preferable)
Step 19: Call “action” function.
I got more than 3.8 BNB in one flash loan

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening emphasizes the title's profit promise and the funding step. Those are real, but its own account says the evidence does not establish what the contract does after confirmation. The surrounding instructions also ask the viewer to create a file, compile code and deploy a contract. A claimed result within that walkthrough is not independent proof of either a genuine return or a fraudulent transfer.

citations.quote: create a file call it contract.sol
Click compile contract.sol
Enter your token details and deploy the contract (MyToken)

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A detailed walkthrough can be the means of solicitation. Here the instructions culminate in sending BNB to the contract and calling its action function, while the speaker says paying more yields more and reports a large return. The fact that the contract's outcome is unverified weakens the claimed demonstration; it does not neutralize the video's instruction to fund a profit-seeking contract.

citations.quote: Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
Call “action” function.
The more BNB you send the more you get

opening.argument: Judge, the transfer instruction is present and should be scrutinized. But the description states a specific operational purpose for the BNB: covering swaps, with an estimated fee range. It directs viewers to deploy a contract, copy the resulting address and use a wallet, rather than identifying a seller or asking them to pay a named person. The supplied material does not establish who controls the resulting address, whether swaps occur or whether anyone receives the claimed return. On this record, a costly contract workflow is visible; the decisive diversion mechanism is not.

citations.quote: New contract will appear under DEPLOYED Contract Field
Copy new contract address generated from the loan pool
Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps
it's going to take around 0.18-0.19 BNB fees

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening establishes that viewers are told to fund a contract while hearing profit claims. It does not establish recipient ownership, actual returns or what the contract does after confirmation, as it acknowledges. The instructions instead describe a deployed contract address and give a swap-fee explanation for the transfer. That explanation is unverified, but so is the allegation that the payment is diverted.

citations.quote: Copy new contract address generated from the loan pool
Send 0.2+ BNB to the contract for gas fee for all swaps

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Unknown recipient ownership does not resolve the central concern. The video tells viewers to fund a contract before calling its action function and explicitly ties the amount sent to what they supposedly receive. Calling the payment a swap fee is part of the video's claim, not verification that swaps occur. The title's easy-profit pitch makes this a solicitation for funded-contract returns, even without proof of a completed diversion.
